title: Mechanical and tribological properties of TiC-SiC-ZrC hybrid carbide-reinforced FeMn 0.25 CrNi high-entropy alloy composites prepared by spark plasma sintering
abstract: Abstract The service environment of high-entropy alloys is becoming more and more extreme, which puts forward more stringent requirements on their comprehensive mechanical properties. Therefore, the development of high-performance composites needs to be promoted urgently. Novel TiC-SiC-ZrC hybrid carbide-reinforced FeMn 0.25 CrNi high-entropy alloy composites were fabricated via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. During sintering, the added carbides completely dissolved and reacted with the matrix to form in-situ nanoscale M 23 C 6  chromium-rich carbides, which uniformly dispersed both intragranular and intergranular. This hybrid reinforcement remarkably refined the grains from 2.28 μm to 0.93–1.07 μm through effective Zener pinning. The optimized Ti2Si2Zr1 composite achieved an exceptional strength-ductility synergy, attaining a yield strength of 1,274 MPa and hardness of 466 HV while retaining 15% strain. Furthermore, the composite exhibited superior wear resistance with a wear rate of 3.6 × 10 –5  mm 3 /Nm, approximately one order of magnitude lower than the matrix alloy. The theoretical yield strength calculated by superimposing multiple strengthening mechanisms showed excellent agreement with experimental results with less than 2% deviation, validating the established strengthening model.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Since their inception in 2004 by Yeh et al. ( 57 ) and Cantor et al. ( 7 ), high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as a frontier in materials science research, distinguished by their unique multi-principal-element design paradigm and exceptional comprehensive properties. Unlike conventional alloys based on a single principal element, HEAs comprise five or more principal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The high configurational entropy effect promotes the formation of simple solid-solution phases (face-centered cubic [FCC], body-centered cubic [BCC], or hexagonal close-packed [HCP]), effectively suppressing the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds (Miracle and Senkov  33 ; George et al.  11 ).This distinctive phase structure endows HEAs with an attractive combination of high strength, high hardness, excellent wear and corrosion resistance, and remarkable thermal stability (Li et al.  22 ; Gludovatz et al.  12 ). Among these HEAs, the FeMnCrNi system has garnered considerable attentions due to its cost-effectiveness, superior biocompatibility, and excellent strength-ductility synergy; notably, these alloys exhibit outstanding yield strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures (Bian et al.  5 ; Zhou et al.  66 ,  67 ).

However, single-phase HEAs often exhibit insufficient strength for extreme service environments. Second-phase strengthening, particularly through in-situ formation of ceramic carbide phases ( TiC, SiC or ZrC), represents an effective strategy to enhance the mechanical performances of HEAs (Lu et al.  27 ; Liu et al.  26 ). The incorporation of carbides significantly improves strength, hardness, and wear resistance through grain boundary pinning and Orowan mechanisms (Mehmood et al.  31 ; Li et al.  23 ; Pritima et al.  44 ; Guo et al.  13 ). Moreover, the synergistic addition of multiple carbides can generate composite strengthening effects, further enhancing the comprehensive properties of the material (Zhang et al.  63 ; Wang et al.  51 ).

Regarding processing methodologies, spark plasma sintering (SPS) has become a prominent technique for fabricating HEA-based composites, characterized by rapid heating, short holding times, and efficient densification (Moravcik et al.  34 ; Pan et al.  39 ). Compared with conventional vacuum arc melting, SPS effectively inhibits grain coarsening, yielding uniform and fine microstructures. Additionally, the pulsed current-induced surface activation of powder particles facilitates in-situ reactions, promoting robust interfacial bonding between the reinforcement and matrix (Moravcik et al.  34 ,  34 ; Pan et al.  39 ,  39 ; Pohan et al.  43 ; Xi et al.  54 ; Hu et al.  19 ).

With respect to strengthening mechanisms, systematic investigations have elucidated the synergistic interactions among solid-solution strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, and precipitation strengthening in HEAs (Basu and Hosson  3 ). For carbide-reinforced systems, nano-sized carbide precipitates and grain refinement collectively enhance mechanical properties, with operative mechanisms involving the interplay between Orowan bypass and shear mechanisms (Xie et al.  55 ; Gao et al.  10 ; Chang et al.  8 ).

In terms of tribological performances, HEAs and their composites demonstrate excellent wear resistance (Liang et al.  25 ; Zhou et al.  68 ; Wu et al.  53 ). Interstitial strengthening and dispersion strengthening by boron significantly improve high-temperature wear resistance (Zhou et al.  68 ), whereas oxidative wear represents the dominant wear mechanism for refractory HEAs at elevated temperatures (Wu et al.  53 ; Pei et al.  42 ; Cheng et al.  9 ).

FeMnCrNi high-entropy alloys offer significant cost advantages due to the absence of strategic elements such as Co and W, while their single-phase FCC structure confers exceptional fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, rendering them promising candidates for extreme-service applications including liquid-hydrogen storage tanks, aerospace propulsion systems, and nuclear reactor structural components (Gludovatz et al.  12 ; Parkin et al.  41 ). However, their intrinsically low yield strength and inadequate wear resistance severely restrict engineering applicability under heavy-load and wear-coupled conditions. This work systematically validates the feasibility of simultaneous strengthening and wear-resistance enhancement at room temperature via a TiC–SiC–ZrC ternary hybrid carbide reinforcement strategy, providing foundational data and microstructural design guidelines for future performance optimization targeting specific service environments.

In summary, although significant progress has been achieved in HEA-based composites, the mechanism underlying the synergistic strengthening of high-entropy alloys by multiple carbides remains elusive. Therefore, this work aims to elucidate the corresponding synergistic enhancement mechanism. In particular, the influence of multicomponent carbide additions on microstructural evolution, mechanical properties, and tribological behavior remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study employs mechanical alloying combined with spark plasma sintering to fabricate TiC-SiC-ZrC carbide-reinforced FeMn 0.25 CrNi HEA-based composites. The in-situ formation mechanisms of composite carbides, microstructural characteristics, mechanical properties, and tribological behavior are systematically investigated, with particular emphasis on elucidating the strengthening mechanisms and wear mechanisms, thereby providing theoretical guidance for the design of high-performance HEA-based composites.

sections.heading: Materials and process
paragraphs: Commercially available elemental Fe, Cr, Ni, and Mn powders, with purity exceeding 99.9% and initial particle sizes below 25 μm, were employed as raw materials. Based on the nominal composition of FeMn 0.25 CrNi, the metal powders were precisely weighed according to stoichiometric ratios and loaded into stainless steel milling vial. To prevent cold welding during high-energy ball milling, wet milling was conducted using anhydrous ethanol as a process control agent (PCA). Milling was performed in an XQM-4 planetary ball mill with stainless steel balls at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 15:1, a rotation speed of 300 rpm, and a duration of 60 h. Upon completion, the as-milled powders were vacuum-dried, gently ground, and sieved to obtain the final FeMn 0.25 CrNi high-entropy alloy powders.

FeMn 0.25 CrNi HEA powder was employed as the matrix, with TiC, SiC, and ZrC carbides formulated into hybrid reinforcement phases at varying mass ratios, yielding a total addition level of 5 wt.%. To suppress carbide agglomeration and minimize oxygen contamination, the powder mixtures were subjected to high-energy ball milling for homogeneous processing at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1 and a rotation speed of 300 rpm for 36 h. The milled powders were subsequently cold-compacted and consolidated via spark SPS at 1,050 °C under an applied pressure of 60 MPa for 3 min, with a heating rate of 100 °C/min. The entire sintering process was conducted under high vacuum (< 10 –3  Pa) to preclude oxygen incorporation. The key sintering parameters, including the temperature, pressure, and holding time, were optimized through orthogonal experiments. This processing protocol enables rapid densification of the composites while concurrently attaining a synergistic enhancement of mechanical strength and ductility. The as-sintered specimens possessed dimensions of ϕ20 mm × 8 mm. For comparative analysis, the matrix alloy powder was also processed under identical conditions, designated as FeMn 0.25 CrNi. The composites containing TiC-SiC-ZrC hybrid reinforcements are herein denoted as Ti2Si2Zr1 (TiC:SiC:ZrC = 2:2:1) and Zr2Si2Ti1 (ZrC:SiC:TiC = 2:2:1) according to the carbide mass ratios, with detailed compositions listed in Table  1 . Table 1 Composition of mixed powders and composite materials Samples Composition (wt.%) FeMn 0.25 CrNi FeMn 0.25 CrNi Ti2Si2Zr1 FeMn 0.25 CrNi + 2% TiC + 2% SiC + 1% ZrC Zr2Si2Ti1 FeMn 0.25 CrNi + 2% ZrC + 2% SiC + 1% TiC

sections.heading: Characterization methods
paragraphs: The crystal structure of the specimens was characterized using Co-target X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical AERIS). Microstructural morphologies were examined via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, JEOL JSM-7100F) equipped with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) acquisition systems and Channel 5 software employed for quantitative analysis of grain size and carbide distribution. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250XI) was utilized to track the evolution of elemental chemical states during tribological testing.

sections.heading: Determination of density
paragraphs: Multiple measurements were performed for each specimen. After excluding anomalous values, the arithmetic mean of the remaining valid data was adopted as the final result.

sections.heading: Compressive tests
Microstructure
paragraphs: Figure  1  presents the XRD patterns of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy and its Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites fabricated via SPS. All specimens exhibit characteristic diffraction peaks corresponding to an FCC structure. No diffraction peaks from the added carbides (TiC, SiC, and ZrC) were detected within the composites, indicating basically dissolution of these carbides during SPS, with carbon diffusing into the matrix and reacting with Cr to form in-situ M 23 C 6  chromium-rich carbides (Huang et al.  20 ). Trace amounts of M 23 C 6  were identified in the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy, attributable to carburization from the graphite die at elevated temperatures (> 1,000 °C) under the coupled thermal-electrical field of pulsed direct current. Fig. 1 XRD patterns of sintered bulk FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1

Compared with the matrix alloy, the composites exhibit a pronounced shift of principal diffraction peaks toward higher angles, primarily arising from the synergistic effects of substantial interstitial carbon solid solution introduced by carbide dissolution and the volumetric constraint of reinforcements (Ahn et al.  1 ). According to Bragg's law, the contraction of interplanar spacing leads to an increase in the diffraction angle (Tao et al.  48 ). The composites possess significantly higher interstitial carbon concentrations than the matrix alloy, resulting in a marked reduction in FCC lattice parameters. Additionally, the incorporation of Ti, Zr, and Si modifies the electronic concentration and atomic bonding state of the matrix, further inducing lattice contraction. Moreover, residual compressive stresses generated during cooling due to thermal expansion coefficient mismatch between the matrix and reinforcements, superimposed with the constraint effect of high-volume-fraction reinforcements, collectively drive the peak shift toward higher angles.

Figure  2  presents the microstructural morphologies of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy and Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites fabricated by spark plasma sintering (SPS). As shown in Figs.  2 (a)-(c), both Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites exhibit particulate and dispersive distributed carbide phases with varying sizes randomly embedded in the matrix; in contrast, the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy displays a relatively smooth surface without noticeable carbide precipitation (Han et al.  14 ). No significant porosity is found in all three alloys, indicating a high degree of densification achieved by the SPS process. Fig. 2 SEM microstructures of the matrix and composite materials. (a, a 1 , a 2 ) Ti2Si2Zr1; (b, b 1 , b 2 ) Zr2Si2Ti1; (c, c 1 , c 2 ) FeMn 0.25 CrNi

Figures  2 (a 1 )-(c 2 ) present the corresponding high-magnification views of the selected regions. Further examination reveals that the carbide particles in Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites are predominantly nanoscale (< 500 nm) and uniformly dispersed throughout the matrix (Pakhomova et al.  38 ). This homogeneous precipitation of nanoscale carbides can be attributed to the rapid sintering characteristics of SPS, which effectively suppress grain coarsening while promoting the nucleation and dispersive distribution of in-situ reaction carbides. The absence of distinct carbide phases in the matrix alloy confirms that the carbide reinforcements in Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites primarily originate from interfacial reactions and in-situ precipitation between TiC, SiC, and ZrC ceramic particles and the matrix, rather than precipitation from the matrix alloy itself (Nagarjuna et al.  37 ).

Figure  3  presents the backscattered electron (BSE) micrographs and corresponding elemental mapping of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy and Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites. As shown in Fig.  3 a and (b), both Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites exhibit typical multiphase microstructures with pronounced elemental segregation after sintering at 1,050 °C. The bright-contrast regions correspond to the FCC matrix phase enriched with Fe, Cr, and Ni, whereas the dark-gray regions correspond to carbide phases enriched with Ti, Zr, Si, and C. Additionally, trace amounts of unreacted TiC and ZrC particles are found to remain in the matrix. However, no distinct diffraction peaks corresponding to these phases are detected in the XRD patterns. This can be attributed to the relatively low mass fraction of the added TiC and ZrC ceramic particles, combined with their partial consumption during interfacial reactions at elevated sintering temperatures (Mihai et al.  32 ; Zeng et al.  60 ). Fig. 3 SEM backscattered electron (BSE) micrographs and corresponding EDS elemental mappings of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy and Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites. ( a ) Ti2Si2Zr1; ( b ) Zr2Si2Ti1; ( c ) FeMn 0.25 CrNi

EDS elemental mapping results reveal a uniform distribution of Si within the composite matrices, indicating that SiC undergoes sufficient reaction and diffusion with the matrix at high temperatures, leading to the formation of uniformly dispersed silicides or solid-solution strengthening phases. In contrast, the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy shown in Fig.  3 c exhibits a typical single-phase solid-solution microstructure with homogeneous elemental distribution and no evident elemental segregation or secondary phase precipitation. This further confirms that the formation of carbide reinforcing phases in the composites originates from in-situ interfacial reactions between the added ceramic particles and the matrix, rather than solid-state phase transformation of the matrix alloy itself.

Figure  4  presents the EBSD maps of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and its composites (Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1), including inverse pole figures (IPF) and kernel average misorientation (KAM) distributions. Figures  4 (a), (c) and (e) clearly reveal the grain morphology and crystallographic orientation characteristics of each alloy. Compared with the matrix alloy, the synergistic addition of multiple carbides exerts a significant grain-refining effect on the matrix, with average grain sizes of 0.93 μm, 1.07 μm, and 2.28 μm for Ti2Si2Zr1, Zr2Si2Ti1, and FeMn 0.25 CrNi, respectively. In Ti2Si2Zr1, Cr 23 C 6 -type carbides are uniformly dispersed at grain boundaries with a high volume fraction, effectively pinning grain boundary migration and resulting in a more uniform grain size distribution than that of the matrix alloy and Zr2Si2Ti1. Conversely, the grain coarsening is evident in carbide-depleted regions, whereas significant grain refinement occurs in carbide-enriched regions, corroborating the dominant role of the Zener pinning mechanism (Luo et al.  28 ). The average carbide sizes in the Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites are 0.45 μm and 0.50 μm, respectively. Fig. 4 EBSD characterization of the alloy and composites. ( a - b ) IPF and KAM maps of Ti2Si2Zr1; ( c - d ) IPF and KAM maps of Zr2Si2Ti1; ( e – f ) IPF and KAM maps of FeMn0.25CrNi

Figures  4 (b), (d) and (f) reflect the spatial distribution of geometrically necessary precipitation (GND) density in the alloys, with KAM values being positively correlated with local precipitation density. The KAM maps of Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 show that green high-value regions are primarily distributed near grain boundaries and carbide/matrix interfaces, indicating significant local orientation gradients and high precipitation densities in these regions (Zhong et al.  65 ). This strain concentration phenomenon arises from thermal residual stresses induced by the coefficient of thermal expansion mismatch between carbides and the metal matrix, which promotes GND accumulation at interfaces during rapid cooling (Zhou et al.  69 ). In contrast, the KAM map of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy is almost entirely covered by blue low-value regions, indicating minimal local misorientation within coarse grains and at grain boundaries, with GND density significantly lower than that of the composites (Table  2 ). sections.heading: Mechanical behavior
paragraphs: Figure  5 a presents the room-temperature compressive stress–strain curves of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and its composites (Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1), with the corresponding mechanical properties summarized in Table  3 . Both composites exhibit significant enhancement in yield strength compared with the matrix alloy: Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 achieve yield strengths of 1274 MPa and 1156 MPa, respectively, representing increases of 438 MPa and 320 MPa (52% and 38%) over FeMn 0.25 CrNi (836 MPa). Meanwhile, their compressive strains decrease by only 28% and 17.6%, respectively. Notably, Ti2Si2Zr1 exhibits an ultimate compressive strength of 1,944 MPa with a retained compressive strain of 15%, demonstrating an excellent strength-ductility synergy. Fig. 5 Mechanical properties of FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1. ( a ) Room temperature compressive stress–strain curve; ( b ) Micro-Vickers hardness; ( c ) Comparison of the compressive strength and strain of Ti2Si2Zr1 composites prepared in this study with those reported in the literature (Zong et al.  70 ; Yim et al.  58 ; Nagarjuna et al.  36 ; Zhang et al.  62 ; Malatji et al.  30 ; Li et al.  24 ; Hassan et al.  15 ; Qin et al.  46 ; Stepanov et al.  47 ) Table 3 Density of FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 Samples Density (%) Ti2Si2Zr1 97.7 ± 0.17 Zr2Si2Ti1 97.6 ± 0.22 FeMn0.25CrNi 98.3 ± 0.14

Table  3  presents the relative density of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy and the Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites fabricated by SPS. All three specimens achieved relative densities exceeding 97.5%, with the pristine FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy attaining the highest value of 98.3 ± 0.14%, followed by the Ti2Si2Zr1 (97.7 ± 0.17%) and Zr2Si2Ti1 (97.6 ± 0.22%) composites. The marginal decrease in relative density for the composites compared to the matrix alloy is primarily attributed to the hindrance of full pore elimination by the non-deformable ceramic–metal phase boundaries introduced by the hard reinforcement particles, coupled with potential interfacial porosity arising from the in-situ reactions between the carbide precursors and matrix elements. Notably, the Zr2Si2Ti1 composite exhibits a slightly lower density with a larger standard deviation, which may indicate inferior distribution homogeneity of ZrC within this composition. Nevertheless, the achieved relative densities of 97.6–97.7% are fully adequate for structural applications and are comparable to those reported for analogous carbide-reinforced high-entropy alloy composites, validating that the selected SPS parameters effectively balance densification with microstructural control.

Figure  5 b shows the micro-Vickers hardness of the three materials. The FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy exhibits a hardness of 324 HV, whereas Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 reach 466 HV and 448 HV, respectively, corresponding to improvements of approximately 44% and 38%, indicating that carbide incorporation significantly enhances the load-bearing capacity. Figure  5 c compares the compressive yield strength and elongation of Ti2Si2Zr1 with carbide-reinforced high-entropy alloy matrix composites and refractory alloys reported in the literature, revealing that Ti2Si2Zr1 markedly outperforms its counterparts in the strength-ductility trade-off.

sections.heading: Friction and wear behavior
paragraphs: The tribological behavior of the matrix alloy FeMn 0.25 CrNi and the composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 is presented in Fig.  6 a. Under identical sliding conditions, the friction and wear process can be divided into an initial running-in stage and a steady-state wear stage. During the initial running-in period, the coefficient of friction (COF) rapidly increases to a pronounced value, indicating an unstable contact condition; subsequently, after a brief running-in duration, the COF quickly stabilizes with significantly reduced fluctuations, signifying the transition to the steady-state wear stage (Bedolla-Becerril et al.  4 ). The COF values of the three alloys exhibit slight fluctuations during sliding, decrease slightly at approximately 300 s, and eventually stabilize at around 450 s. The steady-state COF values for FeMn 0.25 CrNi, Ti2Si2Zr1, and Zr2Si2Ti1 are determined to be 0.519, 0.475, and 0.522, respectively. Fig. 6 Reciprocating friction and wear behavior of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and the Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites under a normal load of 10 N at a sliding speed of 0.02 m/s. ( a ) friction coefficient as a function of sliding time; ( b ) cross-sectional profiles of the wear tracks; ( c ) average coefficient of friction and wear rate in the steady-state stage

Figure  6 b illustrates the cross-sectional profiles of the wear tracks for the three alloys, while Fig.  6 c summarizes the average COF and wear rates, with detailed results compiled in Table  4 . The incorporation of carbides and their varying addition ratios exert a pronounced influence on the wear performance of the materials. Specifically, Ti2Si2Zr1 demonstrates superior wear resistance with a wear rate of (3.6 ± 0.382) × 10 –5  m 3 /Nm, which is approximately half that of Zr2Si2Ti1 (7.755 ± 0.445) × 10 –5  mm 3 /Nm and one order of magnitude lower than that of FeMn 0.25 CrNi (16.7 ± 0.424) × 10 –5  mm 3 /Nm. The wear rates of the three materials exhibit an inverse relationship with their hardness (Figs.  5  and  6 ), consistent with Archard equation (Archard  2 ), which states that volumetric wear loss is inversely proportional to the material hardness. The matrix alloy exhibits the deepest and widest wear scar with substantial fluctuations in the cross-sectional profile, indicating that FeMn 0.25 CrNi undergoes severe wear accompanied by increased surface roughness. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to intensive ploughing effects and adhesive wear. In contrast, the two carbide-reinforced composites exhibit markedly reduced surface damage, which can be ascribed to the precipitation of ceramic phases that substantially enhance the strength and hardness of the composites, thereby mitigating damage induced by high contact stresses. Table 4 Compression properties and hardness of FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 Samples Yield strength (MPa) Ultimate compressive strength (MPa) Fracture strain (%) Hardness (HV) Ti2Si2Zr1 1274 ± 18.3 1944 ± 11.4 15 ± 0.6 466 ± 9.3 Zr2Si2Ti1 1156 ± 13.3 1932 ± 10.7 17.3 ± 1.9 452 ± 8.8 FeMn 0.25 CrNi 836 ± 12.2 1606 ± 13.9 21 ± 1.3 324 ± 18.6

The superior wear resistance of the Ti2Si2Zr1 composite over Zr2Si2Ti1 originates from the synergistic coupling of microstructural refinement and tribochemical stability. Relative to Zr2Si2Ti1, Ti2Si2Zr1 exhibits a higher Vickers hardness (466 HV versus 452 HV), a refined grain size (0.93 μm versus 1.07 μm), and a reduced carbide size (0.45 μm versus 0.50 μm), with the grain size also being substantially lower than that of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix alloy (2.28 μm). This hardness enhancement and microstructural refinement effectively suppress abrasive plowing, consistent with the inverse hardness–wear rate relationship described by the Archard equation. Concurrently, a denser oxide layer formed on the worn surface of Ti2Si2Zr1 affords a lower steady-state coefficient of friction (0.475, significantly below 0.522 for Zr2Si2Ti1), thereby effectively alleviating adhesive wear.

To gain deeper insight into the evolution of wear mechanisms, the wear surface morphologies of the matrix alloy FeMn 0.25 CrNi and the composites Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 were systematically characterized, as shown in Fig.  7 . Under a normal load of 10 N, the parallel grooves aligned with the sliding direction, wear debris, microcracks, and obvious layered spalling were available on the worn surfaces of all three alloys. Combined with EDS point analysis (Table  5 ), slight oxidation traces were detected on the worn surfaces, indicating that the dominant wear mechanisms were abrasive wear accompanied by mild adhesive wear. Fig. 7 Wear surface morphology and element distribution of matrix alloy FeMn 0.25 CrNi and composite materials Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1. ( a ) Ti2Si2Zr1; ( b ) Zr2Si2Ti1; ( c ) FeMn 0.25 CrNi Table 5 Average coefficient of friction and wear rate of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and the Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites Samples Average friction coefficient Average wear rate (× 10 –5  mm 3 /Nm) Ti2Si2Zr1 0.475 ± 0.017 3.6 ± 0.382 Zr2Si2Ti1 0.522 ± 0.008 7.755 ± 0.445 FeMn 0.25 CrNi 0.519 ± 0.002 16.7 ± 0.424

Figures  7 (a)-(c) present the SEM micrographs of the worn surfaces. Comparatively, the composites exhibited significantly less wear damage than the matrix alloy. Although all three samples displayed grooves, debris accumulation, cracks, and delamination features, the matrix alloy showed higher crack density, more pronounced debris accumulation, and reduced spalling area. This is attributed to the compaction of warped oxide flakes on the wear surface, which prevented the material from reaching the critical threshold for spalling. Therefore, the primary wear mechanisms for FeMn 0.25 CrNi and both composites at room temperature were abrasive wear and mild adhesive wear.

At this stage, adhesive wear manifested predominantly as delamination. Similar to the Al 0.5 CoCrCuFeNi HEA (Wu et al.  52 ), the worn surfaces underwent periodic delamination fracture: the asperities on the Si 3 N 4  counterpart ball continuously cut the material to generate wear debris, inducing abrasive wear; meanwhile, reciprocating compression led to oxidation and hardening of debris at elevated temperatures. As debris continued to indent the surface, tensile stresses generated upon reaching the critical indentation depth initiated crack nucleation, forming both longitudinal cracks perpendicular to the surface and transverse cracks propagating from the subsurface toward the surface. When transverse cracks intersected or propagated to the surface, the material loss occurred as delamination (Zhang et al.  64 ). Table  5  reveals abundant fragmented lamellar oxide glaze layers on the alloy surfaces, with large-area oxidation evident on the worn surfaces. When the load was increased to the threshold for oxide layer fracture, the dominant wear mechanism transitioned to adhesive wear combined with oxidative wear (Lv et al.  29 ).

For the Ti2Si2Zr1 composite, the fracture rate of the oxide film was lower than its formation rate, resulting in the development of a dense oxide layer on the wear surface that effectively reduced the friction coefficient and wear rate. This represents the fundamental origin of its excellent wear resistance (Table  6 ). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was conducted on the worn surface of the Ti2Si2Zr1 composite to determine its chemical composition. The high-resolution XPS spectra are presented in Fig.  8 . Figure  8 a shows the XPS spectrum of Ti2Si2Zr1, which clearly shows that Fe, Mn, Cr, Ni, O and C elements can be detected before and after friction and wear. Notably, the oxygen content on the worn surface increased significantly, as evidenced by the enhanced intensity of the O 1s peak, indicating the occurrence of friction-induced oxidation. The frictional heat generated during the wear process led to partial oxidation of the material surface. Combined with the high oxygen content observed in the wear debris (Fig.  7 ), these results confirm the presence of an oxidative wear mechanism and the formation of substantial metal oxides, including Fe 3 O 4 , Fe 2 O 3 , FeO, MnO, Mn 2 O 3 , MnO 2 , Cr 2 O 3 , CrO 3  and NiO. Fig. 8 High-resolution XPS spectra of Ti2Si2Zr1 composite surface before and after wear. ( a ) Survey; ( b ) Fe 2p; ( c ) Mn 2p; ( d ) Cr 2p; ( e ) Ni 2p

Figure  8 b shows the characteristic peaks of the Fe 2 p  spectrum, revealing the valence state information of iron on the worn surface. After wear, the fitted peaks at 709.5 eV and 723.2 eV correspond to the Fe 2 p 3/2  and Fe 2 p 1/2  energy levels of Fe 2+  (FeO), while the fitted peaks at 711.0 eV and 724.6 eV correspond to the Fe 2p 3/2  and Fe 2 p 1/2  energy levels of Fe 3+  (Fe 3 O 4 /Fe 2 O 3 ), respectively. Notably, the intensity of the metallic Fe 0  peak decreases significantly, indicating the partial oxidation of iron during the friction process. Figure  8 c presents the Mn 2 p  spectrum, which exhibits a complex valence state distribution encompassing Mn 2+  (MnO), Mn 3+  (Mn 2 O 3 ), and Mn 4+  (MnO 2 ). This multivalent characteristic demonstrates the high reactivity of manganese during the friction process. The Cr 2 p  spectrum (Fig.  8 d) is dominated by a prominent peak at 575.5 eV, corresponding to Cr 2 O 3 . The superior chemical stability of this chromium oxide renders it the primary constituent of the surface protective film (Hu et al.  18 ). In contrast, the Ni 2 p  spectrum (Fig.  8 e) reveals that metallic Ni 0  remains the dominant species, with characteristic peaks at 852.3 eV (Ni 2 p 3/2 ) and 869.9 eV (Ni 2 p 1/2 ). The NiO component appears at 853.8 eV with relatively low intensity, reflecting the chemical inertness of nickel. These findings demonstrate that friction and wear induce the formation of a multilayered tribo-oxidation film comprising an outer layer of Fe–Mn oxides, an intermediate layer of Cr 2 O 3 , and an inner layer enriched in Ni, which significantly influences the tribological performance of the material (Bian et al.  6 ).

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The strength of metal matrix composites (MMCs) is typically governed by the particle size of reinforcements, their distribution uniformity, and the interfacial bonding state with the alloy matrix. In this study, the incorporated carbide reinforcements can form favorable interfacial bonding with the alloy matrix via spark plasma sintering. More importantly, owing to the consistently small particle size of carbides during the incorporation process, combined with high-energy ball milling and short sintering holding time, the carbide particle size remains stabilized at a relatively low level. Furthermore, the three types of carbides exhibit relatively uniform dispersion around the alloy grains, thereby exerting a significant strengthening effect. The following sections will elaborate on the evolution behavior of carbides, the formation mechanism of well-bonded interfaces, the distribution characteristics of carbides, and their influence on mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Sintering mechanism
paragraphs: The Gibbs free energy is calculated to be -381 kJ/mol (Huang et al.  20 ). Compared with the fine SiC, TiC, and ZrC particles, the formed Cr 23 C 6  carbide exhibits a significantly larger size.

When the Ti2Si2Zr1 composite was sintered at 1,050 °C by SPS, favorable interfacial contact was established between the ex-situ carbides and matrix. The SPS process, characterized by pulsed-current-induced localized surface activation and rapid solidification, promotes intimate contact between the reinforcement and the matrix, favoring the formation of low-mismatch metallurgical bonding interfaces. Figure  9  illustrates the interfacial evolution mechanism between the carbides and the FeMn 0.25 CrNi matrix during SPS sintering. In the initial stage, pulsed current excites plasma generation at the gaps between pre-compacted powder particles, inducing discharge phenomena and elevating the local surface temperature of the particles. As the temperature rises rapidly, the FeMn 0.25 CrNi particles undergo localized melting and rapidly achieve metallurgical bonding with the surfaces of adjacent carbide particles under axial pressure. Once effective connection between the matrix and carbides is established, the micro-discharges dissipate immediately, and the localized high-temperature region cools down rapidly. Owing to the minimal lattice mismatch between the matrix and carbides, the molten matrix tends to heterogeneously nucleate on the carbide surfaces, thereby forming well-bonded interfaces (Zeng et al.  60 ). As depicted in Fig.  9 c, numerous nanoscale carbide particles migrate into the outer molten layer of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi particles driven by surface tension. Subsequently, the micro-discharges cease, and the molten zone solidifies. Evidently, the carbide particles provide abundant heterogeneous nucleation sites during solidification, thereby effectively promoting grain refinement (Zeng et al.  61 ). Fig. 9 Illustrates the unique spark plasma sintering and consolidation process of carbides with the HEA matrix

sections.heading: Strengthening mechanisms
paragraphs: Upon the incorporation of composite carbides, the mechanical properties of the composites were significantly enhanced compared to those of the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy (Table  3 ). SEM/BSE observations reveal that nanoscale carbides are uniformly distributed within grains and at grain boundaries, with no evident voids or debonding signs observed at the interfaces, indirectly indicating a relatively favorable interfacial bonding state, playing a pivotal role in the strengthening mechanism. Meanwhile, the hard carbides with high thermal stability effectively suppressed the migration and coarsening of FeMn 0.25 CrNi grains during sintering. As shown in Table  2 , with the addition of different proportions of composite carbides, the average grain sizes of Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 were remarkably refined from 1.92 μm to 1.07 μm and 0.93 μm, respectively. The reduced grain size provides a higher grain boundary area fraction, thereby effectively impeding precipitation motion and enhancing mechanical strength.

The Ti2Si2Zr1 composite exhibits an exceptionally high yield strength of 1,274 MPa at room temperature. The aforementioned analysis reveals the presence of multiple secondary phases in this composite, with significant variations in their types, contents, and distribution characteristics. These secondary phases, whether distributed intragranular or intergranular, effectively impede precipitation slip. Furthermore, the grain refinement strengthening effect arising from the suppression of the grain growth by secondary phases contributes additionally to the enhancement of yield strength. The high strength of the Ti2Si2Zr1 composite results from the synergistic contribution of multiple strengthening mechanisms, including grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening, Orowan mechanism, and solid solution strengthening.

Based on calculations using Eq. ( 4 ), the theoretical yield strength of the ternary carbide-reinforced high-entropy alloy matrix composite prepared in this study is determined to be 1,291 MPa. As illustrated in Fig.  10 , the discrepancy between the theoretical prediction and experimental measurement is approximately 30 MPa, corresponding to a relative error of less than 2%, which demonstrates excellent agreement between the strengthening mechanism model and the experimental results. Specifically, grain refinement strengthening contributes 431 MPa, accounting for nearly 30% of the total strengthening effect; the Orowan bypass mechanism associated with second-phase particles contributes 438 MPa; while precipitation strengthening and solid solution strengthening contribute 438 MPa and 85 MPa, respectively. In the development of ceramic particle-reinforced HEA composites, full advantage should be taken of the synergistic effects among grain refinement strengthening, Orowan strengthening, and solid solution strengthening to achieve superior comprehensive mechanical properties. Fig. 10 Statistics of experimental and theoretical yield strength contribution of Ti2Si2Zr1 composites

sections.heading: Friction and wear mechanisms
paragraphs: For the FeMn 0.25 CrNi alloy and Ti2Si2Zr1 and Zr2Si2Ti1 composites, the wear process exhibits distinct stage-dependent evolution characteristics. In the absence of mixed carbides, the grinding ball readily undergoes mechanical interlocking with the alloy surface during friction, inducing localized stress concentrations at surface defects and consequently generating cracks and plowing grooves. Under the action of frictional heat, Fe, Mn, and Cr react with oxygen to form a dense oxide layer that serves a dual function of lubrication and oxygen isolation, thereby effectively reducing the friction coefficient. However, the addition of minor amounts of mixed carbides introduces hard phases such as Cr 23 C 6  and increases surface roughness, which paradoxically elevates the friction coefficient and promotes oxide layer thickening. Once the oxide layer reaches a critical thickness, it becomes susceptible to delamination under shear stress owing to its inherent brittleness. Furthermore, localized stresses generated by asperity contact under load can induce brittle fracture of Si 3 N 4  grinding balls, creating hard abrasive particles that exacerbate the wear process. As wear progresses, these abrasives gradually wear down, and the contact mode transitions from point contact to surface contact, consequently diminishing the cutting effect on the alloy. Notably, SiC, TiC, and ZrC particles play a pivotal role during wear: due to their higher hardness relative to the matrix, these particles preferentially contact the abrasives to form friction pairs, generating a "protective effect" that effectively suppresses wear propagation. In the later wear stages, fractured carbide particles and matrix debris decompose under elevated temperatures, whereupon SiC, TiC, and ZrC combine with matrix elements to form new Cr 23 C 6  carbide phases, further enhancing matrix hardness.

Given that materials operate under high-temperature conditions during friction and wear processes, temperature exerts a decisive influence on wear mechanism transitions. At room temperature, Ti2Si2Zr1 alloy undergoes primarily abrasive wear, with hardness serving as the critical controlling parameter; this alloy exhibits superior hardness owing to high-volume-fraction carbide phases, high-hardness ceramic precipitates, and lattice distortion strengthening, resulting in reduced wear severity. As wear progresses and interfacial temperature rises, the alloy yield strength decreases due to thermal softening, and the adhesion fracture energy diminishes, causing the wear mechanism to gradually transition toward adhesive wear and promoting interfacial adhesion (Yu et al.  59 ).

In summary, the wear mechanisms of Ti2Si2Zr1 alloy primarily encompass oxidative wear and adhesive wear: oxidative wear persists throughout the process, abrasive wear dominates the initial stage, and adhesive wear becomes predominant in later stages. The tribological behavior of these alloys represents the coupled consequence of intrinsic material properties, microstructural evolution, and environmental conditions. Through regulation of hard phase content, optimization of interface characteristics, and consideration of service temperatures, controllable transitions in wear mechanisms can be effectively achieved, providing theoretical foundations for the design of high-performance wear-resistant alloys (Zeng et al.  60 ).

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In this study, TiC-SiC-ZrC hybrid carbide-reinforced FeMn 0.25 CrNi high-entropy alloy matrix composites were fabricated via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. The synergistic strengthening mechanisms governing the mechanical properties were systematically elucidated, while the evolution characteristics and underlying wear-resistant mechanisms of the tribological behavior were revealed. The principal conclusions are summarized as follows: In-situ carbide formation and grain refinement. During spark plasma sintering, the added TiC, SiC, and ZrC carbides completely dissolved and reacted with the matrix to form nanoscale M 23 C 6  chromium-rich carbides that uniformly dispersed both intragranularly and intergranularly. This hybrid carbide reinforcement remarkably refined the matrix grain structure from 2.28 μm to 0.93-1.07 μm through effective Zener pinning, providing increased grain boundary area to impede precipitation motion. Exceptional strength-ductility synergy. The Ti2Si2Zr1 composite achieved a superior combination of mechanical properties, attaining a yield strength of 1,274 MPa and hardness of 466 HV while retaining 15% stress. This enhancement originates from the synergistic contributions of grain boundary strengthening (~ 431 MPa), Orowan mechanism (~ 438 MPa), solid solution strengthening (~ 85 MPa), and precipitation strengthening. Significantly improved wear resistance. The Ti2Si2Zr1 composite exhibited a wear rate of 3.6 × 10 −5  mm 3 /N m, approximately one order of magnitude lower than the matrix alloy. The dominant wear mechanisms were abrasive wear accompanied by mild adhesive wear, with the formation of a dense oxide tribolayer effectively reducing friction and protecting the surface. Multiple strengthening contributions, is in excellent agreement with the experimental result (1,274 MPa), with only a minor deviation. This close correspondence strongly corroborates the reliability of the established strengthening model for the carbide-reinforced high-entropy alloy matrix composites.
